rationale: A wins because it stays inside the facts and gives the founder a usable sequencing call: pitch pricing only after getting the executive rationale, hold the accuracy story until audit data exists. Its headline "A $12B payroll company just made AI compliance a free feature, not a product" is a clean business-model angle, while B's "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" quietly invents prior pricing and a competitive category. B has good lawyerly questions, but it keeps turning gaps into claims; that is how a pitch becomes a corrections file.
gaps_in_A: "One employer, one bad contractor call" is useful but not pitchable from the supplied update alone; A admits "Without a named customer there is no story at this rung."

"A $12B payroll company just made AI compliance a free feature, not a product" is slightly ahead of the facts; the update only says included for existing customers, not permanent, free for new customers, or not a paid product elsewhere.
"Story type: funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the pricing angle. There is no funding event; this is business model or AI monetization.
gaps_in_B: "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" invents prior pricing. The update says the AI tool is included for existing customers, not that Deel used to sell this layer separately.
"compresses the ground under standalone compliance vendors" invents a competitor landscape and market impact. No standalone vendors, pricing response, or competitor product facts were supplied.
"The prevailing belief in the category is that AI can now absorb compliance work" is a made-up straw peg unless B can source it. The update does not contain that belief.
The first two kept angles are too close: "with no accuracy numbers" and "Who eats the fine when the AI misclassifies a contractor?" are both the same accuracy-liability story with a different jacket.
